lesson.title: When Farmers Took Up Arms Against Their Own State
lesson.summary: Shays' Rebellion, an armed uprising of debt-ridden Massachusetts farmers in 1786 and 1787, exposed the Articles of Confederation's inability to respond to internal unrest and pushed American leaders toward a stronger national government.
lesson.body:
The government created by the Articles of Confederation had proven too weak to manage debts and foreign relations, but by 1786 that weakness had turned into something more alarming: it could not even keep order at home. In western Massachusetts, farmers who had fought in the Revolutionary War found themselves crushed by debt, high state taxes imposed to pay off Massachusetts's own war bonds, and a state government in Boston that seemed indifferent to their suffering. Courts were foreclosing on farms and throwing debtors into prison at an alarming rate.

Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain who had fought at Bunker Hill and Saratoga, emerged as one of the leaders of the resulting uprising, though he was never its sole mastermind and the movement drew leaders from several Massachusetts counties. Beginning in the fall of 1786, armed farmers began shutting down county courts across western Massachusetts to physically prevent judges from issuing foreclosure orders. What started as scattered local protest grew into a more organized movement by the winter of 1787, alarming a state government that had few tools ready to respond.

The rebellion reached its climax on January 25, 1787, when a force of roughly fifteen hundred men marched on the federal armory at Springfield, hoping to seize weapons. Militia under General William Shepard defended the armory and fired cannon into the approaching rebels, killing several and scattering the rest. Massachusetts Governor James Bowdoin then raised a larger militia force, funded privately by worried Boston merchants since the state treasury was strained and the Confederation Congress could offer no meaningful help. That militia, commanded by General Benjamin Lincoln, pursued and dispersed the remaining rebels over the following weeks.

What made Shays' Rebellion so significant was not the uprising itself but what it revealed. The Confederation Congress had watched a domestic insurrection unfold in one of its largest states and had essentially no capacity to respond, no national army to call on and no funds to raise one quickly. George Washington, then living in retirement at Mount Vernon, was reportedly deeply alarmed, worried that the entire republican experiment might collapse into chaos or, worse, invite a return to monarchy if it could not maintain basic order.

The rebellion gave urgent, concrete force to arguments that had already been building since the Treaty of Paris exposed Congress's weakness. It directly strengthened the case for the Annapolis Convention's call for a broader meeting to fix the Articles of Confederation, a meeting that would convene in Philadelphia just months later and quickly become something far more ambitious than anyone had planned.

Even delegates who might otherwise have resisted a stronger national government found it hard to argue for the status quo after Springfield. If a state as established as Massachusetts could nearly be overwhelmed by its own citizens, and the national government could do nothing but watch, then the case for revising or replacing the Articles of Confederation had moved from theoretical to urgent almost overnight.
